utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. To begin, would I just like to ascertain and make sure the Court has the new list of witnesses for this week. It's the same witnesses as the former list, with one exception; we are eliminating the former number 2 in an attempt to streamline, that would be John Wall, who would not have been a protected witness, and the new order is as now listed on the new list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In addition, I would like to inform the Court that over the weekend the Victim and Witnesses Unit contacted me with a message from the witness that we had last week, who requested that he be allowed to look at the diary or the log that was discussed on cross-examination, and as I recall during the cross-examination of that witness, he had some difficulty recognising it as his, it was a Xerox copy, two pages were on a single sheet of Xerox paper, and there was some discussion about allowing him to have some time to look at the original. I think there was an understanding at that time that there was, in fact, an original having been submitted in another case for identification. Our understanding now is that, in fact, there is no original yet submitted in that other case. The copy was not submitted for evidence, it was submitted for only identification at this point, although I think there's some indication that there will be a witness in that case to introduce that diary at a later date. The witness has not had an opportunity to study the Xerox copy, except for the short amount of time he had during cross-examination. So the Victim and Witnesses Unit did convey that message to me, and I convey that to the Court. I request that the Court grant him an opportunity to look at the Xerox copy and give him sufficient amount of time to do that so that he can make a determination about whether he authored some or all of that diary. In connection with that though, I would like to also raise Rule 95 with the Court and with Defence counsel, which refers to evidence that is obtained in a way that is -- would throw doubt on its reliability or on the integrity of the proceedings. I raise that Rule to stress that I think that it might be useful for the Court to determine, as an initial matter, how that diary came into the possession of the Defence, whether, in fact, it came into position in some illegal manner, through a theft, through an illegal search of this man's home. The evidence indicates this man was forced from his home, and if he was illegally forced from his home, as I think the evidence shows, and then these very same people then entered his home and did a search, there may be some issue with respect to Rule 95. At least as an initial matter, it may be useful to make that inquiry to get an idea of where this diary came from. The reliability of this diary as a piece of evidence, I think, though, ultimately depends upon who wrote it, and whether the witness can identify and then offer explanations. But I think, as an initial matter, Rule 59 might have to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I would like to apologise for giving information which was wrong on Friday. That is to say I thought that the diary was either with General Blaskic's Defence or in the records, but as I know that they filed -- whether the diary was with the file or not. So there was a misunderstanding, and I'm very sorry for that. I did not want to cast any doubt on anybody, but I just did not have information available. I would like to say, with regard to how the diary was found and the circumstances governing that, that we talked to a witness called Ivica Vidovic Jevco. He is from Ahmici, and he found the diary -- that is to say his son found the diary, and he will be a witness in this case. So the circumstances governing the diary and how it was found, we'll be able to hear it directly from the testimony of the witness. After that, the witness handed over the diary to the Vitez Brigade, and a copy of that diary we received later on and we have the not seen the original of the diary. I have asked the counsel of General Blaskic to tell me where the original is located at the moment, but they referred to client-attorney privilege, and so they were not able to supply me with that information. But we will, of course, for our part, try to find out where it is, because we know how important the diary is. For the moment, we can say -- we'll be able to say whether the facts correspond to what was brought up here by the witness on Friday, that is to try to ascertain -- to identify the diary on the basis of the facts, and, therefore, we would like to have our proposal that we have a graphological examination of the handwriting if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course, the graphological information, the expertise, can all be made on the original. So if we don't have the original, we won't proceed to such expertise. Let us see. Then I would like to -- I'm sorry, I regret that the -- over the weekend the witness was not given an opportunity to take a look at the photocopy. This was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think there was some confusion, Mr. President, at the end of the day. He had a -- the photocopy that was marked, the Court's evidence, in front of him. He did not take it, and I think there was some confusion about whether he should look at the photocopy or the original, and there was a discussion about the original. I, frankly, thought he had the photocopy. When I realised he didn't, it was too late to come back to the Court, everyone was dispersed. Then when he communicated to us through the Victim and Witnesses Unit, I think our only recourse at that time was to wait until the Court convened to alert you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Shall we go on with the evidence of the witness? Now, we have decided that we will -- to save time, we will now ask the registrar to hand over a copy of the diary to the witness so that he can have time to go through it, a copy of the Bosnian original, and meanwhile, we go on with another witness, and later on we will resume the cross-examination of this particular witness. So we move on to witness number 2 on our new list. I think, Mr. Terrier, you wish to attribute a pseudonym to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This will be the Witness W, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please stand and read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to hand to you a sheet of paper on which your name appears. Could you please confirm that it is your name that appears on the sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Once again the diacritic is missing on the C. The diacritic above the C in two places, in his name and the end of his surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We do apologise, Mr. Radovic. Your Honour, I wonder if maybe it will be a good thing to go at once into closed session. This would enable me to give you a number of identifying elements on this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness has requested protection of face and name, and she will be Witness X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Could you push up your chair up a little closer to the microphone so we can hear you well? Thank you. At this time I will hand to the usher the next Prosecution exhibit, which is a slip of paper with a name on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 223.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness, you have asked for protection measures and they have been granted by the Court. So we are going to refer to you as Witness X rather than by using your name. During the course of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- if it's necessary to talk about certain things that might give away your identity, we will ask to go into closed session, and if the Tribunal agrees to that then in closed session your voice will not leave this room and you can feel comfortable to provide full and complete testimony at that point as well. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you first tell us what year you were born in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And up until April 16, 1993, where did you live, in what village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I lived in Ahmici, at Zume. I lived there up till the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Without giving us any names, could you tell us the family members who lived with you during those days before April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: My husband (redacted), my daughter (redacted), my daughter (redacted), my daughter (redacted) and my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best to go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: My son (redacted). (Closed session).

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: 1.29 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of September, 1998, at 9.30 a.m.
